candidate_analysis.explanation: The Random Forest assigned MALWARE with probability 1.0000, and all 20 listed n-grams push toward cryptojacking. However, the evidence is thin. No function names, API calls, strings, or per-function locations were supplied, so nothing ties these n-grams to a mining routine. Most x86 n-grams (CMOVZ MOV, ADD POP, XOR CALL, AND MOV, CALL ADD, CALL XOR, TEST JZ, XOR SHL, MOV JZ, CMP JL, SUB LEA, XOR XOR, XOR CMOVNZ, ADD BLX) have a displayed frequency of 0.000000, so they are rare or negligible in the binary. The ARM-style n-grams (eor sub, mvn orr, sub strb, and ldrh, orr bic, cmn mov) have small but nonzero frequencies; sub strb is the highest at 0.001004. The mix of x86-style uppercase and ARM-style lowercase mnemonics suggests multiple architectures or a feature set spanning both, but this alone says nothing about cryptojacking. The XOR-related patterns (XOR CALL, CALL XOR, XOR SHL, XOR XOR, XOR CMOVNZ, eor sub) and the bitwise patterns (mvn orr, orr bic, and ldrh) are loosely consistent with the bit-mixing and hashing arithmetic seen in proof-of-work or cipher code, but they are also common in compression, checksums, obfuscation, and ordinary compiler output. Individual SHAP values are small (+0.0048 to +0.0114), with no dominant feature, so the verdict is the sum of many weak signals. The model's confidence is high, but the supplied evidence cannot confirm mining behavior, so the finding is suggestive rather than conclusive.
